content: The document outlines the contributions of various experts and organizations involved in the development of WHO guidelines for the treatment of non-severe hypertension during pregnancy. 1. Dr. Ebun Adejuyigbe, a Consultant Neonatologist from the Department of Paediatrics and Child Health at Obafemi Awolowo University in Nigeria, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 2. Dr. Shabina Ariff, a Consultant Paediatrician and Neonatologist from Aga Khan University in Karachi, Pakistan, also served as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 3. Jemima Dennis-Antwi, an International Consultant in Midwifery based in Accra, Ghana, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 4. Luz Maria de-Regil, Founder and President of Nutrition Developments in Ottawa, Canada, contributed as a content expert and end-user. She disclosed a grant support from the Government of Canada to her former employer, Nutrition International, for a research study. This conflict was deemed not significant enough to affect her participation. 5. Professor Christine East, a Professor of Nursing and Midwifery at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 6. Lynn Freedman, Director of the Averting Maternal Death and Disability Program at Columbia University in New York, USA, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 7. Professor Pisake Lumbiganon, a Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Khon Kaen University in Thailand, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 8. Anita Maepioh, a Nurse Educator from the National Referral Hospital in Honiara, Solomon Islands, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 9. Dr. Shireen Meher, a Consultant in Maternal Fetal Medicine at Birmingham Women’s and Children’s NHS Foundation Trust in the UK, disclosed her role as the chief investigator of a randomized controlled trial evaluating calcium supplementation for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women. This conflict was not considered significant enough to affect her participation. 10. Professor James Neilson, from the Department of Women’s and Children’s Health at the University of Liverpool, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 11. Hiromi Obara, Coordinator of the Life-Course Health Team at the National Center for Global Health and Medicine in Tokyo, Japan, participated as a content expert and implementer. No conflicts of interest were declared. 12. Dr. Cristina Palacios, an Associate Professor in the Department of Dietetics and Nutrition at Florida International University in Miami, USA, conducted a landscape review for WHO on the global status of calcium fortification. She also disclosed her role as an investigator on a grant studying the effects of soluble corn fiber supplementation on bone metabolism in adolescents. 13. Rachel Plachcinski, a Research Engagement Officer at the National Childbirth Trust in London, UK, served as a consumer representative. No conflicts of interest were declared. 14. Zahida Qureshi, an Associate Professor in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Nairobi in Kenya, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 15. Professor Kathleen Rasmussen, a Professor of Maternal and Child Nutrition at Cornell University in Ithaca, USA, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 16. Niveen Abu Rmeileh, Director of the Institute of Community and Public Health at Birzeit University in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, contributed as a content expert and implementer. No conflicts of interest were declared. 17. Eleni Tsigas, Chief Executive Officer of the Preeclampsia Foundation in the USA, represented patient experiences related to pre-eclampsia and other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. This conflict was not considered significant enough to affect her participation. 18. Caroline Homer, Co-Program Director of Maternal and Child Health at the Burnet Institute in Melbourne, Australia, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 19. Hadiza Galadanci, Director of the Africa Center of Excellence for Population Health and Policy at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 20. Jashodhara Gupta, Executive Director of the National Foundation for India in New Delhi, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 21. Professor Jack Moodley, Head of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 22. Dr. M Jeeva Sankar, Assistant Professor at the WHO Collaborating Centre for Training and Research in Newborn Care at AIIMS in New Delhi, India, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 23. Professor Shakila Thangaratinam, from Birmingham Women’s and Children’s NHS Foundation Trust in the UK, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 24. Saraswathi Vedam, an Associate Professor in the Midwifery Program at the University of British Columbia in Canada, contributed as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. 25. Professor Hayfaa Wahabi, Chair of Evidence-Based Healthcare at King Saud University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, participated as a content expert and end-user. No conflicts of interest were declared. This document also includes detailed assessments of antihypertensive drug interventions for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy, focusing on maternal and fetal outcomes such as maternal mortality, eclampsia, pre-eclampsia, severe maternal morbidity, ICU admissions, adverse effects, and neonatal outcomes like perinatal death, NICU admissions, and Apgar scores.
